A child who was growing along the 15th percentile (P15) for weight-for-age (WFA) until the age of 4 years and 2 months experienced a weight loss of 2 kg over a 6-month period, dropping from 15 kg to 13 kg, which represents a 13% reduction in body weight. 2. Another child, aged 1 year and 10 months, had been growing along the 50th percentile (P50) for WFA until the age of 1 year and 6 months. However, over the past 4 months, this child lost 3 kg, with their weight decreasing from 10 kg to 7 kg, equating to a 30% weight loss. Their WFA Z-score fell below -3, which is significantly below the 3rd percentile (P3). The most critical observation in this case is the trajectory of weight loss over the past 3 months. 3. Children who maintain growth along the same percentile line for many years, even if their WFA Z-score is more than 2 standard deviations below the norm, are not typically a concern for tuberculosis (TB) disease. A Z-score of -2 indicates underweight for age, while a Z-score of -3 indicates very low WFA. 4. Pulmonary TB in children can present atypically, such as with acute severe pneumonia, which is more common in children under 2 years of age and those living with HIV. Fixed airway wheezing is another atypical presentation, more frequently observed in children under 5 years of age. Signs of pneumonia include cough or difficulty breathing accompanied by tachypnea (fast breathing) or chest indrawing, along with danger signs such as inability to breastfeed or drink, persistent vomiting, lethargy, reduced consciousness, convulsions, stridor in a calm child, or severe malnutrition. 5. TB should be suspected in cases of poor response to antibiotics, particularly if there is a history of contact with a TB-positive individual. In children living with HIV, other HIV-related lung diseases, such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (formerly known as Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia or PCP), should also be considered. 6. Asymmetrical and persistent wheezing in children may result from airway compression caused by enlarged intrathoracic TB lymph nodes. Other symptoms, such as poor weight gain or persistent fever, may also indicate TB. Weight loss or failure to thrive should raise suspicion. Wheezing due to asthma is typically recurrent and variable, responds to inhaled bronchodilators, and is not associated with other typical features of TB. 7. Despite challenges in bacteriological confirmation of paucibacillary TB in young children, every effort should be made to establish bacteriological confirmation. Adolescents, who often present with adult-type TB disease, are more likely to have bacteriological confirmation. 8. WHO-recommended clinical samples for diagnosing pulmonary TB in children and adolescents using Xpert MTB/RIF or Ultra include sputum (expectorated or induced), gastric or nasopharyngeal aspirates, and stool. Other molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) have only been validated on sputum samples. 9. Older children and adolescents with adult-type TB disease (e.g., cavitation on chest X-ray) often test positive on bacteriological testing. Sputum collection through spontaneous expectoration is feasible in these age groups, typically from about 8 years of age, though sometimes in younger children. 10. The choice of specimen type depends on factors such as acceptability for the child, parents, and healthcare workers; feasibility of collection and preparation in the local context; and local test availability. 11. Stool is a newly recommended specimen for diagnosing TB in children using Xpert MTB/RIF or Ultra. It is particularly useful when obtaining adequate respiratory specimens is challenging, such as in younger children. Stool testing is less invasive than gastric or nasopharyngeal aspiration and may be more acceptable and feasible in certain settings. 12. Children with TB often swallow sputum containing TB bacilli from the lungs, which then pass through the digestive tract and can be detected in stool samples. Therefore, stool is considered a respiratory specimen for TB diagnosis. 13. When using stool specimens, a pre-processing step is required before inserting the sample into the Xpert cartridge. Preliminary data suggest that the Simple One-Step (SOS) method is the easiest to implement in lower-level laboratories and is the most cost-effective while maintaining diagnostic accuracy. 14. Nasopharyngeal aspiration (NPA) is a relatively simple procedure that is less invasive than gastric aspiration and carries a lower risk of nosocomial transmission compared to sputum induction. It can be used in children unable to spontaneously expectorate sputum, especially in settings where more invasive procedures are not feasible. 15. NPA involves suctioning the nasopharynx using a sterile catheter inserted into the child’s nostril while the child is in a supine position. The procedure requires fasting for 2 hours beforehand and often necessitates additional support to restrain the child during the procedure. 16. The TB-Speed Decentralization study assessed the impact of decentralizing an innovative childhood TB diagnostic approach in six countries with high TB incidence. The intervention included systematic TB screening, clinical evaluation, NPA and stool or sputum testing using Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra, and optimized chest X-ray reading. 17. The TB-Speed Pneumonia study evaluated the feasibility and yield of Ultra testing on stool samples in children with severe pneumonia. The study found that combined NPA and stool samples were safe, highly feasible, and contributed to microbiological confirmation in 30% of children diagnosed with TB. 18. Most parents perceived NPA as a painful and fearful procedure for their child but maintained positive attitudes toward it, trusting the nurses’ skills and understanding its aim to improve child health. Nurses also viewed NPA as unpleasant but necessary for improving child health and reducing mortality. 19. NPA was successfully performed in 95% of children, and combined NPA and stool samples were effective in confirming TB microbiologically in a significant proportion of cases. Despite its perceived discomfort, NPA was considered acceptable and feasible for TB diagnosis in children.
